analysis.one_liner: Bans health plan contract clauses that stop doctors from telling patients about treatment options and costs.
analysis.headline: With 303 House cosponsors — 167 Democrats, 135 Republicans, and 1 Independent — the bill never received a committee vote or floor action in two years.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for health plans to put "gag clauses" in their contracts with doctors — provisions that stop doctors from telling patients about treatment options, utilization review rules, or financial incentives that might affect their care. States would enforce the rule against health insurers, with the federal government stepping in if a state failed to, and the Labor Department covering plans that states cannot reach. The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in managed care and other health plans would gain a federal guarantee that their doctors can freely discuss their health status, treatment options, utilization review requirements, and any financial incentives that might affect their care [S2][S3]. Doctors and other licensed providers would also benefit, since gag clauses in their plan contracts would be null and void [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes null and void any contract provision between a health plan and a provider that prohibits or restricts the provider's medical communications with the patient.

'Medical communication' is defined broadly to cover discussions of the patient's health status, treatment options, any utilization review requirements affecting treatment, and any financial incentives that may affect the patient's treatment.

Each state must enforce the ban against health insurers selling plans in the state; if a state fails to substantially enforce it, the Secretary of Health and Human Services steps in and can impose civil money penalties of up to $25,000 per violation.

Plans exempt from state regulation under federal employee-benefit law would be covered by enforcement from the Secretary of Labor, closing a gap that would otherwise leave many employer plans untouched.

The bill does not preempt state laws that are equally or more protective of doctor-patient communication, and it preserves plans' ability to enforce quality and utilization-review programs as long as those programs do not restrict medical communication.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care companies would bear the cost: they could no longer write contract clauses restricting what doctors tell patients, would face civil money penalties of up to $25,000 per violation for plans they operate, and would face federal enforcement through HHS or the Labor Department if a state failed to enforce the law [S2][S3]. Indirectly, insurers argued such rules constrain how they manage care and could add administrative costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

drawbacks.text: The bill only protects what doctors may say; it does not limit what plans may actually cover or deny, so patients could still be told about a treatment the plan would not pay for.

Plans may still require providers to cooperate with utilization review and quality programs, as long as those programs do not restrict medical communication — a line that plans could test in practice.

The bill expressly allows a plan to tell providers and enrollees about limitations on services based on the plan's religious or moral convictions, which critics could view as permitting plans to steer patients away from certain care.
Enforcement depends on state insurance regulators acting first, with federal backup only after HHS determines a state has failed to substantially enforce the law, which could leave gaps in practice.
Insurers would face compliance costs and civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation, costs that honest supporters would acknowledge are real even if they serve patient interests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is real but modest in scope: it guarantees that doctors can speak freely about treatment options, utilization review, and financial incentives, and it closes the employer-plan enforcement gap. The bill deliberately does not touch what plans cover or deny, so it protects information rather than care itself, and it carves out room for utilization-review programs and religious or moral disclosure. Against a low cost to insurers — removing gag clauses and facing penalties for violations — the bill would likely have shifted information and some leverage to patients without changing benefit design. The larger story is what did not happen: with more than two-thirds of the House signed on, it never got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees for two years without a single vote, and the Congress ended with it still stuck there.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 5, 1997 and referred to three committees at once — Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce — rather than one.
Within two weeks it was sent to three subcommittees: Health, Health and Environment, and Employer-Employee Relations.
Over the following two years, the record shows no committee vote, no markup, and no floor action — the only activity after referral was the sponsor's introductory remarks in March 1998.
Despite 303 cosponsors — 167 Democrats, 135 Republicans, and 1 Independent — the bill never came to a vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care companies came out ahead: no law restricted their contracts with doctors, so they kept the contractual tools this bill would have voided. No patient received any protection from the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care companies

for.name: Rep. Greg Ganske
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor in March 1998.

for.name: 303 of 435 House members
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — 167 Democrats, 135 Republicans, and 1 Independent — roughly seven in ten members of the House.

against.name: Speaker Newt Gingrich
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to three separate committees at once, a routing decision that split its consideration and contributed to it stalling without any committee vote.

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce committees
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled it for action in the two years after referral; the only subcommittee referral was in February 1997 and nothing followed.

against.name: Health insurers and HMO industry
against.role: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on managed care contracts during the late-1990s patients' rights debate, in which gag-clause bans like this bill figured prominently.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was strongly bipartisan: 167 Democrats and 135 Republicans (plus 1 Independent) signed on as cosponsors, but the Republican-run committees and leadership never allowed a vote on it.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care companies
industries.note: The bill would strike down contract clauses letting plans silence doctors about treatment options, utilization review, and financial incentives, and would impose civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation. The industry's interest in keeping those tools ran directly against patients' ability to learn about care they might need.

Self-insured employer plans would fall under Labor Department enforcement of the ban, an added compliance obligation, though the bill explicitly leaves the rest of the federal employer-plan law untouched.

industries.industry: Physicians and licensed health care providers
industries.note: Doctors would be freed from contract language restricting what they could say to patients, though the bill preserves plans' ability to enforce evidence-based utilization review and bars doctors from misrepresenting covered benefits.
